sections.title: Campaign Overview
sections.content: May 2026 was a month that revealed a great deal about where the security questionnaire market currently sits. The overall tone across conversations was polite but largely deflective — prospects were rarely hostile, but a significant portion had either already found a way to manage the problem or didn't see it as a pressing enough pain point to warrant a conversation. The market feels crowded at the solution layer, with many companies having invested in tooling, internal processes, or workarounds that give them just enough coverage to feel comfortable, even if those solutions are imperfect.
sections.content2: Where genuine conversations did land, there were clear signals of relevance — contacts who acknowledged the questionnaire burden, who are actively building solutions of their own, or who sit adjacent to the problem in ways that could develop into longer-term opportunities. The two meetings booked and six activations suggest that when the right contact was reached with the right framing, the proposition resonated. The challenge this month was less about the message and more about penetrating organisations to reach the people who actually feel the pain.
sections.content3: A recurring theme was navigational friction — reaching gatekeepers, automated systems, wrong contacts, and individuals on leave or simply unavailable. This points to a data and targeting opportunity rather than a fundamental message problem. The prospects who did engage and declined mostly did so because they had already addressed the issue, which is a useful signal in itself: Securilix is fishing in the right pond, but needs sharper hooks to catch those who haven't yet solved the problem.

rows.what_said: Directly named by a prospect as their current solution for managing security questionnaires, used alongside AI tooling. Prospect felt fully covered with no gaps.

Multiple prospects referenced AI-based approaches — one had automated their questionnaire process entirely using AI and considered themselves ahead of the curve. Another was building a 'home-baked solution' with AI components.

Several prospects described having internal thresholds, compliance teams, or proprietary workflows that handle questionnaires with minimal volume reaching the sales team. One noted 'strict internal thresholds and deal with very few requests now.'
One prospect was actively building a public trust centre to streamline their questionnaire process, describing it as effective for engaging with both large enterprises and smaller distributors.
A prospect mentioned being on an 'anecdote supplies list' which effectively removed the questionnaire burden from their sales team entirely.
One contact at a security consultancy described using a mixed approach with software solutions to manage questionnaires for their own clients, suggesting they operate in an adjacent space.

items.objection: Already have a tool or process in place
items.quote: They already use Vanta and AI tools, effectively managing their questionnaires. Jack feels fully covered and sees no gaps in their current solution.
items.analysis: This was the dominant objection of the month and cuts across company sizes and sectors. It suggests that whilst the problem is real and recognised, many organisations have made at least a first-generation investment in solving it. The opportunity lies in probing the quality and completeness of those solutions — many 'workarounds' or internal processes are brittle and don't scale. Repositioning the conversation around the gaps, edge cases, and audit trail limitations of DIY solutions could unlock more of these conversations.

items.objection: Not relevant — we don't receive security questionnaires
items.quote: They don't receive security questionnaires as they don't sell to businesses, so my solution isn't relevant.
items.analysis: A meaningful subset of contacts simply don't operate in a context where security questionnaires arise — they sell direct to consumers, operate in closed ecosystems, or sit in sectors not subject to enterprise procurement scrutiny. This is a targeting signal. Filtering the contact list more aggressively towards B2B SaaS, fintech, and regulated-sector vendors would reduce wasted dials on this cohort.

items.objection: Low volume — not a significant enough problem
items.quote: They receive security questionnaires infrequently (2-6 times every few months). They have found a workaround, indicating it's not a significant issue for them.
items.analysis: Some prospects acknowledge receiving questionnaires but don't experience sufficient volume for it to constitute a pain point. These contacts are not the right target profile right now, but could become so as their business scales. A light-touch nurture sequence rather than continued cold outreach would be more appropriate for this group.

items.objection: Not the right person / not my area
items.quote: The security questionnaires aren't his area. He suggested I reach out to either Andy Hunter (CSO) or Stuart Hall (main DRC engineer) for the best assistance.
items.analysis: A significant number of calls landed on contacts who acknowledged the problem exists in their organisation but own it somewhere else — compliance teams, CSOs, or dedicated engineers. Positively, some of these contacts provided referrals, which is valuable. The focus should be on converting these moments into warm introductions rather than ending the call, and ensuring the CRM captures every named referral for immediate follow-up.

items.quote: He was busy with other priorities but agreed to check the company website for more information.
items.analysis: A cluster of prospects weren't philosophically opposed but simply couldn't engage in the moment. These are not lost opportunities — they are deferred ones. The key is ensuring there is a reliable follow-up cadence attached to every 'call me back' or 'send me an email' response, with a specific date and channel agreed before ending the call.

items.question: Can you send information over email or to the website?
items.analysis: Prospects who weren't ready to commit to a conversation but weren't entirely dismissive defaulted to requesting email follow-up. This reveals a degree of curiosity paired with time pressure — they want to evaluate on their own terms. It is worth treating these as warm signals and ensuring any follow-up email is concise, value-led, and includes a clear call to action for a specific date.

items.question: Who are you and why are you calling?
items.analysis: The high frequency of this through gatekeepers and initial contact moments underlines that Securilix does not yet have strong brand recognition in this market. It is a reminder that the opening seconds of a call need to establish relevance immediately — not just company name, but a sharp statement of the problem being solved.

items.question: Is this relevant to our type of business?
items.analysis: A small number of prospects actively questioned whether the solution applied to their context, suggesting the outreach may not always have been sufficiently tailored to their sector or business model before dialling. More targeted list segmentation and a brief contextual hook in the opener that references their specific situation could reduce this and increase early engagement.

items.heading: The 'solved it ourselves' trap
items.body: A striking number of prospects have built or adopted first-generation solutions — AI tools, internal compliance workflows, public trust centres — and believe the problem is resolved. Many of these solutions are unlikely to be robust at scale, but prospects do not yet feel the gaps. The market is in a phase where initial adoption has occurred but dissatisfaction with those solutions has not yet matured into active re-evaluation.

items.heading: Navigational friction is masking real demand
items.body: A large proportion of calls this month did not reach the intended decision-maker at all — gatekeepers, automated systems, wrong contacts, and absent individuals dominated the connected-call landscape. This is not a rejection of the proposition; it is a data and access problem. Improving contact accuracy and decision-maker identification before dialling would likely unlock a meaningfully higher conversation rate from the same dial volume.

items.heading: Referrals are an underutilised asset
items.body: Several calls resulted in named referrals to CSOs, compliance leads, and specialist engineers — contacts who are far closer to the questionnaire pain than the individuals originally dialled. These moments are currently being treated as neutral outcomes, but they represent warm pathways into better-qualified contacts. Capturing and acting on every referral systematically could significantly improve meeting quality.

items.heading: Timing and priorities are genuine blockers
items.body: Beyond tool adoption, a recurring theme was simply that prospects were mid-project, short-staffed, or focused on other quarters. One was on paternity leave, another mid-product build, another consistently caught at a bad time. This suggests a pipeline of contacts who may be open in Q3 or Q4 and who would benefit from a structured re-engagement sequence rather than repeated cold outreach.

items.heading: The B2B vs. B2C targeting gap
items.body: A notable number of contacts disqualified themselves on the basis that they do not sell to businesses and therefore do not receive enterprise security questionnaires. This segment is consuming dial capacity without any realistic conversion potential. A tighter ICP filter focused on B2B SaaS and technology vendors operating in regulated or enterprise-facing sectors would improve the proportion of genuinely relevant conversations.

sections.title: Recommended Actions
items: Implement a structured referral capture protocol — every call where a prospect says 'that's not my area' should end with a named contact and, where possible, a warm introduction or permission to reference the conversation. The CSO and DRC engineer names provided by Yanis this month are exactly the kind of leads that should be in active follow-up immediately.

Tighten the target list to exclude B2C and non-enterprise-facing businesses — a meaningful volume of dials this month reached contacts for whom security questionnaires are structurally irrelevant. Filtering the list to B2B SaaS, fintech, and regulated-sector technology vendors will increase the proportion of relevant conversations per dial.

Develop a specific rebuttal for the 'we already have a tool' objection — this was the most common blocker in May. A short, sharp line of questioning around scalability, audit trails, and the cost of engineer time spent on questionnaire responses could open cracks in apparent satisfaction. Prospects who say they are 'fully covered' often have not stress-tested that coverage.

Build a Q3/Q4 re-engagement sequence for 'not right now' prospects — several contacts were open in principle but blocked by timing, live projects, or internal transitions. Rather than cold-calling them again, a structured email and LinkedIn sequence timed to land in late June and early July would keep Securilix visible without requiring dial capacity.

Audit contact data quality before the June campaign — the volume of gatekeepers, automated systems, wrong numbers, and unavailable contacts suggests the underlying list needs refreshing. Validating job titles, direct lines, and company details for at least the top-priority accounts before dialling would reduce wasted attempts and improve the connected-call rate.

spiced.situation: Mark is the Global Defence & Security Director at Basis Technologies, a small (~180 person) SAP partner company selling SAP software to defence agencies globally. His role is sales-focused — he runs their global defence business and sells software to defence agencies across GB and NATO. The company holds ISO 27001 and Cyber Essentials Plus certifications. Mark is not the CISO or a technical security person — he is a sales leader who encounters security compliance as part of the sales process. He acknowledged there is no dedicated security director at the company, meaning security questionnaire ownership is unclear internally.
spiced.pain: Mark immediately recognised what security questionnaires are and showed genuine intrigue, suggesting this is a real and familiar friction point. The company operates in the defence and regulated sector, meaning they are likely subject to demanding compliance requirements including FedRAMP in the US, NATO-related accreditations, and defence-specific clearance frameworks — all of which generate complex, time-consuming questionnaires. Mark could not clearly identify who internally would own this problem ('I can't quite see who I would push you onto'), which itself signals a pain point: there is no clear process or ownership for handling inbound security questionnaires.
spiced.impact: No specific revenue figures or deal losses were cited, but the context is high-stakes: Basis Technologies sells into defence agencies across NATO and the US, where procurement processes are heavily compliance-driven. The SDR's framing — that questionnaires can take 3–7 days or weeks to complete, leaving competitors to submit RFIs and RFPs first — clearly resonated with Mark, who did not push back on it. In a defence sales context, losing ground in a competitive RFP cycle due to slow compliance responses could mean losing significant government or enterprise contracts. The risk is both competitive (being slower than rivals) and reputational (appearing unprepared to regulated buyers).
spiced.critical_event: No hard deadline or specific regulatory trigger was explicitly mentioned. However, Mark referenced several compliance frameworks relevant to their business — FedRAMP, NATO accreditations, Cyber Essentials Plus, ISO 27001 — which suggests ongoing and evolving compliance obligations. He said 'there are things that are coming up' without specifying what those are. The AE should probe this directly on the Monday call to determine whether there is an upcoming procurement, audit, accreditation renewal, or new defence contract pursuit driving urgency.
spiced.decision: Mark is a sales leader, not a technical or security decision-maker. He was candid that he is 'not in any way, shape or form' the security questionnaire owner. He struggled to identify who internally would be responsible, which suggests either the function is distributed or underdeveloped. He expressed personal curiosity and said it was 'worth investigation,' implying he could be an internal champion but is unlikely to be the sole decision-maker or budget holder. The AE needs to uncover who handles compliance and security documentation at Basis Technologies — likely someone in IT, InfoSec, or operations — and determine whether Mark has the influence or appetite to bring them into the conversation.

objections.objection: Mark immediately said he was physically walking out the door to a doctor's appointment and his son's birthday — he was not available to speak.
objections.response: The SDR handled this well. Rather than pushing through, he asked a qualifying question ('If I told you it was about security questionnaires, is it worth calling you back?') which kept the door open without wasting Mark's time. This was an effective pattern interrupt that prompted Mark's curiosity rather than his resistance.

objections.objection: Mark initially said he was not the right person — 'I'm selling SAP software, effectively' — distancing himself from security questionnaire ownership.
objections.response: The SDR broadened the framing to explain that Securilix works with sales-side people receiving questionnaires that slow down the sales cycle. This reframe landed well and shifted Mark from dismissive to curious. However, the SDR did not fully close the loop on who the right internal contact might be — this remains unresolved.

objections.objection: Mark could not identify who internally should own this problem: 'I can't quite see who I would push you onto.'
objections.response: This was left unaddressed. The SDR did not probe further to help Mark think through who might be responsible — an IT manager, a compliance lead, or a bid/tender team member, for example. The AE must pick this up on the Monday call and help Mark map the internal stakeholder landscape.

handovers.recommended_approach: Open by acknowledging the rushed nature of the first call and thank Mark for making time on a Monday. Briefly recap what was discussed to show continuity — reference that he mentioned ISO 27001, Cyber Essentials Plus, FedRAMP, and NATO accreditations specifically, so he knows the AE has been properly briefed and isn't starting from scratch. The strongest angle here is the defence sales cycle: Mark is a sales director selling into defence agencies, so frame Securilix's value in terms of competitive speed in RFP and RFI processes — losing ground to a competitor because a questionnaire took two weeks to complete is a tangible, credible risk in his world. Avoid leading with technical compliance language; lead with sales velocity and deal risk. Early in the call, probe the 'things that are coming up' comment — ask directly whether there is a specific contract pursuit, accreditation renewal, or new market entry (e.g. FedRAMP for US defence work) that is making this timely. This is the most likely route to surfacing a Critical Event. Separately, help Mark identify the right internal stakeholder — suggest that in companies without a dedicated security director, it is often the IT manager, bid manager, or head of operations who ends up owning questionnaire responses. Offer to involve that person in a follow-up if appropriate. Do not oversell on this first meeting — Mark's interest is genuine but exploratory. The goal is to confirm the pain is real, find the internal owner, and identify whether there is a near-term trigger that justifies moving forward.
key_quotes: I am slightly intrigued, actually — security... are you talking about accreditations in the defence space, that kind of stuff?
We haven't got a security director. But this is why I'd like to explore it because there are things that are coming up.
I can't quite see who I would push you onto. If you see what I mean. But I — it was worth — I certainly work for the investigation.
FedRAMP in America — I mean just GB or across NATO.

contact.jobTitle: Head of Information Security and Compliance

spiced.situation: Karen Haydon is Head of Information Security and Compliance at Just After Midnight, a 24/7 operation (likely a managed services or digital operations company based on the domain). She is the sole owner of security questionnaire responses — there is no team or tooling supporting her. She handles a mix of formats: portal-based questionnaires, standalone documents, RFPs, and due diligence questionnaires (DDQs). She attempted to build an internal answer bank herself but never had time to complete it. No existing third-party solution or trust centre is in place. She receives questionnaires from clients across multiple regions and jurisdictions globally.
spiced.pain: Karen is being buried by security questionnaires — she completed 16 in the year to date by mid-May, including five in February and five in March. She currently has three on the go within a single week. Individual questionnaires range from 10–30 minutes for simple ones up to four full days for complex ones — she cited one that had 326 questions and another that was a full RFP with a 150-page terms and conditions document she had to read in full before responding. A core frustration is the nuance required: many questionnaires are project-specific, requiring internal conversations to confirm what services are actually being provided before she can answer accurately. Others arrive via portals with requirements to upload supporting documents, redact sensitive policies, or confirm agreement with the client's own attached documentation. She also flags that questionnaires arrive while she is in external audits with do-not-disturb active, and stakeholders still demand same-day or next-day turnaround.
spiced.impact: The questionnaire burden is directly crowding out Karen's core responsibilities. She explicitly listed internal auditing and security process updates as work that has fallen behind. The time cost is significant — four days on a single questionnaire is not unusual for her. There is also a sales cycle implication: Just After Midnight's ability to close deals is dependent on Karen completing these responses, and delays or errors could jeopardise contracts. The regional and jurisdictional complexity adds compliance risk — each new geography brings unfamiliar legislation she must interpret before she can respond. She described the situation as something that has been on her list for 'a very long time' with no resolution in sight, suggesting this is a sustained operational drag rather than a temporary spike.
spiced.critical_event: No hard deadline, regulatory trigger, or budget cycle was mentioned explicitly. However, the current volume — three questionnaires in one week, 16 already in 2026 by mid-May — suggests the problem is live and acute right now rather than theoretical. The backlog of internal audits and security updates she referenced implies there is mounting pressure building alongside the questionnaire workload. No specific event was cited that would force a decision by a particular date.
spiced.decision: Karen appeared to be the primary decision-maker and the sole user of any solution — she owns the problem entirely and booked the meeting on her own authority without mentioning needing sign-off from anyone else. No budget figure, procurement process, or additional stakeholders were referenced. The decision process appears straightforward at this stage, but this has not been confirmed. It is worth the AE probing whether there is a line manager, finance approval, or procurement step involved before any commercial conversation.

objections.objection: Many questionnaires come in via portals, not as standalone documents — implying the tool may not be able to interact with them directly.
objections.response: Sean acknowledged this but did not address it substantively. He moved past it quickly by emphasising the human element of the service. This remains unresolved and Karen returned to it at the end of the call, listing portals and format variety as a key consideration. The AE must address this directly — Karen needs to understand specifically how Securilix handles portal-based submissions.

objections.objection: Answers are often project-specific and require internal conversations to determine what services are actually being provided — meaning a static answer bank is insufficient.
objections.response: Sean handled this reasonably well, explaining that the service is fully customised per client and not a one-size-fits-all AI output, and that the human review layer exists precisely for this reason. Karen appeared satisfied with this response. The AE should reinforce this point with a concrete example or case study if available.

objections.objection: Some questionnaires require Karen to read and formally confirm agreement with attached client policies and terms and conditions documents before she can respond.
objections.response: Sean acknowledged this was a common scenario but did not explain how Securilix actually handles it — he said he would 'get an answer' for her. This is a live, unresolved question the AE must come prepared to answer. Karen flagged it as something she would be 'interested' to understand, which signals it is a meaningful part of her use case.

objections.objection: Policies and internal documents often cannot be shared externally — Karen needs to share only a contents page or redacted version, which requires judgement about what is and is not disclosable.
objections.response: Sean acknowledged this briefly but did not explain how the service navigates document sensitivity or confidentiality. The AE should be ready to address how Securilix handles restricted documentation and what the data sharing and confidentiality model looks like.

handovers.recommended_approach:
Open by referencing the specifics Karen shared on the call — do not make her repeat herself. She explicitly said she would not hold Sean to remembering everything, but she will respond well to an AE who clearly has been thoroughly briefed. Start with something like: 'I understand you had one questionnaire alone that took four days, and you are currently managing three at once — I want to make sure we are showing you something that actually fits the complexity you are dealing with, not just the straightforward cases.' This signals you have listened and sets the right tone.

The demo must address her four specific scenarios directly: (1) portal-based questionnaires — be explicit about what Securilix can and cannot do here; (2) project-specific responses that require internal alignment before answers can be confirmed — show how the human review layer accommodates this rather than just asserting it does; (3) documents attached by clients requiring formal confirmation of agreement — come with a clear answer, not a vague 'we can look into it'; (4) policy redaction and document sensitivity — explain the confidentiality model and what access Securilix requires.

Probe on volume trajectory. She had 16 questionnaires by mid-May 2026, with five each in February and March. Ask whether she expects this to grow as Just After Midnight wins more business, particularly in new regions — this could strengthen the commercial case significantly.

Probe on decision-making. She booked independently but no one else was mentioned. Ask directly: 'Is this something you would be in a position to move forward on yourself, or would others need to be involved?' Do this early to avoid a late-stage stall.

Quantify the time cost together during the meeting. She mentioned four days on one questionnaire, 326 questions on another, and a 150-page T&C document on a third. Work with her to estimate total hours lost per month — this will make the ROI conversation concrete and personal rather than theoretical.

Do not oversell automation. Karen is sophisticated and already understands the limitations of pure AI responses. She will be sceptical of anything that sounds like a generic AI tool. Lead with the human oversight and customisation angle, and use the AI tooling as a supporting capability rather than the headline.
key_quotes: I spent about four days on one. Oh my God, it's hideous.

It's not as simple as setting something up and saying these are going to be all the answers — it's project specific, it comes down to internal conversations about what services we've actually agreed to provide.
One of them was a full RFP and it had a 150-page terms and conditions document I had to read.

I'd be interested actually as well in what you do about documentation that is sent with those that has to be read — even with due diligence things, they'll attach some of their own policies and terms and conditions and part of the response is please confirm you've read that and you're all right with it.

conversationSummaries.notes: Spoke with James Biggin, who noted they've dealt with security questionnaires and he's been part of that process. However, he mentioned they don’t have the budget to explore solutions this year. He suggested I follow up in a year as their needs might change, but he believes their current volume of requests is not significant enough to warrant a new platform right now.
conversationSummaries.summary: James flagged familiarity with security questionnaires but stated there is no budget to explore solutions this year. Current request volume is considered too low to justify a new platform. He suggested a follow-up in roughly 12 months if circumstances change.
conversationSummaries.signalReason: No budget and volume too low to justify a platform

conversationSummaries.notes:
I spoke with James at Secure Alex. He mentioned the defense industry hasn't modernized, leading to manual processes for security questionnaires. He acknowledges using supplier portals for submissions but expressed interest in our solution for handling these questionnaires faster. We discussed the potential relevance of our service for their needs, and he seemed open to further conversation.


was curious and went to the website. They sell into defense but have an internal team who apparently need specific clearance?
For their non-defense customers they usually log into their portals.
conversationSummaries.summary: A contact at SecureCloud+, which sells into the defense sector, acknowledged that the industry still relies on manual processes for security questionnaires and expressed interest in handling them faster. He was curious enough to visit the website after the call. The defense-sector context and open posture suggest genuine relevance.
conversationSummaries.signalReason: Acknowledged manual pain and proactively visited the website

conversationSummaries.notes: I spoke with John, who informed me that they already have tools in place for handling security questionnaires, specifically using a tool called Vanta. He felt my solution wasn't relevant to their current needs and mentioned they also provide a trust center for compliance information. No further steps were discussed.
conversationSummaries.summary: John at Quorum Cyber already uses Vanta for security questionnaires and supplements it with a trust center for compliance information. He saw no gap that Securilix could fill and dismissed the solution as irrelevant. No next steps were discussed.
conversationSummaries.signalReason: Committed to Vanta with no perceived gap

conversationSummaries.notes: Spoke with Gary, who mentioned that they currently don't face issues with security questionnaires but would like to discuss it further when he’s less busy. He indicated that this matter falls under the compliance team. We agreed to schedule a meeting in a couple of weeks to explore this topic further.
conversationSummaries.summary: Gary at Kao Data does not currently experience pain around security questionnaires and noted that compliance ownership sits with a separate team. Despite this, he was willing to explore the topic further and agreed to schedule a meeting in a couple of weeks. The engagement was polite and mildly open-ended rather than driven by urgency.
conversationSummaries.signalReason: No active pain but agreed to a follow-up meeting

conversationSummaries.notes: Spoke with Jack, who mentioned they handle everything internally and currently have no budget for outsourcing. He’s overwhelmed with sales calls and suggested it would be best not to pursue this conversation further. No next steps discussed.
conversationSummaries.summary: Jack at Entrepreneur First handles everything internally and has no budget for external solutions. He expressed frustration with the volume of sales calls he receives and explicitly asked not to be contacted further. No next steps were discussed.
conversationSummaries.signalReason: Explicitly asked not to be pursued further

conversationSummaries.notes: Called regarding security questionnaires but the prospect indicated it's not relevant to them. They do not handle these requests, and no further interest was shown. I will not follow up with this individual.
conversationSummaries.summary: Celine at Priavo Security indicated that security questionnaires are not part of their operations, making the offering fundamentally irrelevant. No interest was shown at any point during the call. The rep confirmed they will not follow up.
conversationSummaries.signalReason: Security questionnaires are not part of their business

conversationSummaries.notes: Rowan mentioned that while my call was relevant, they are not looking to purchase any services at the moment since they've already implemented automation with AI tools. They indicated they have created their own solution for handling security questionnaires, and there are no short-term changes anticipated. I wrapped up the call and thanked them for their time.
conversationSummaries.summary: Rowan at SurrealDB acknowledged the call was relevant but confirmed they have already built their own AI-driven solution for security questionnaires. No short-term changes are planned, and they are not in the market for external tools. The call ended cordially with no next steps.
conversationSummaries.signalReason: Built a proprietary solution with no plans to change

conversationSummaries.jobTitle: Head of Information Security and Compliance
conversationSummaries.notes: I called to discuss security questionnaires but the prospect was too overwhelmed with work. They asked me to call back early next week once they have a couple of tasks out of the way.
conversationSummaries.summary: Karen at Just After Midnight was too busy to engage but did not dismiss the topic. She asked to be called back early the following week once she had cleared some tasks. No pain or interest was articulated beyond the callback request.
conversationSummaries.signalReason: Standard timing deferral with no signal on interest

conversationSummaries.notes: Called Mark to discuss security questionnaires for new clients, but he was on another work call. He suggested I call back at a later time as he isn't the best person for this matter. I need to follow up and possibly find the correct contact for this topic.
conversationSummaries.summary: Mark at Instinct was mid-call and unavailable to speak, and he also indicated he is not the right contact for security questionnaire topics. A follow-up call is needed while also identifying the correct internal contact. No substantive discussion took place.
conversationSummaries.signalReason: Wrong contact, needs re-routing with no signal on fit

conversationSummaries.notes:
Had a cold call with Jay. He mentioned he's working on a home-baked solution for handling security questionnaires, indicating potential competition. He’s busy with other priorities but agreed to check the company website for more information. I’ll follow up with an email to provide details without hitting spam filters.


he's "home baking" his own solution but has better things to be doing so is interested. He was in the hospital with his daughter who has chicken pox and signal was horrendous so asked for an email. I'll ring him back nw as well.


Hi Jay, good speaking with you just now.

As mentioned, we're speaking to businesses who sell to regulated industries or large enterprise orgs and receive a lot of security questionnaires.

This invariably takes people away from doing their jobs and slows down sales cycles.

Securilix offers a 24-hour turnaround time on complex questionnaires and RFIs. Simply forward them to us and we do the rest based on your internal evidence.

Is this worth a conversation to see how it would compare with what you're building?

Thanks and all the best for your daughter
conversationSummaries.summary: Jay at Genesis Global is currently building an in-house solution for security questionnaires but acknowledged he has higher-priority work, signalling the DIY path is a burden. He agreed to check the Securilix website and consented to a follow-up email. The personal circumstances noted in the call suggest care is needed in timing the follow-up.
conversationSummaries.signalReason: DIY solution acknowledged as low priority; open to follow-up

conversationSummaries.jobTitle: Head of Service and Information Security
conversationSummaries.notes: Called Jack at Securelix to discuss security questionnaire challenges. He mentioned they already use Vanta and AI tools, effectively managing their questionnaires. Jack feels fully covered and sees no gaps in their current solution. Concluded the call, recognizing that I was not offering any new value.
conversationSummaries.summary: Jack at Coniq uses Vanta combined with AI tooling and considers his questionnaire process fully automated with no gaps. He saw no additional value in what Securilix could offer and the call concluded without next steps. The existing stack makes displacement unlikely.
conversationSummaries.signalReason: Fully covered by Vanta and AI with no perceived gaps

conversationSummaries.notes: Spoke with Becky who mentioned they've automated their security questionnaire process using AI, making it no longer an issue for them. She indicated they're ahead in this area, and my solution is not relevant. I acknowledged their progress and wished her a great weekend.
conversationSummaries.summary: Becky at Mypinpad has already automated her security questionnaire workflow using AI and considers the problem solved. She viewed Securilix as irrelevant given their current maturity in this area. The call ended amicably but with no path forward.
conversationSummaries.signalReason: AI automation already in place, problem considered solved

conversationSummaries.jobTitle: General Counsel, Head of Risk & Compliance
conversationSummaries.notes: I reached out to Kate at her personal number for a cold call. She mentioned they don't face issues with security questionnaires because they're on an anecdote supplies list, which keeps their sales team from having to deal with them. I offered to help her opt-out of the database, and she expressed thanks for the information.
conversationSummaries.summary: Kate at Birdie explained that being on an approved supplier list means their sales team rarely encounters security questionnaire requests, removing the core pain point. She engaged politely around the opt-out process but showed no interest in the solution itself. The structural reason for low questionnaire volume makes this a poor fit.
conversationSummaries.signalReason: Approved supplier status eliminates the core pain point

conversationSummaries.notes: I reached out to Barry Shaw for a cold call about security questionnaires. He was out to lunch and indicated that it wasn't a good time to talk. He agreed to have me call back next week, either on Monday or Tuesday.
conversationSummaries.summary: Barry at TransACT was out to lunch and unavailable for a substantive conversation. He agreed to a callback on Monday or Tuesday of the following week. No objections or interest signals emerged from the brief exchange.
conversationSummaries.signalReason: Timing deferral only, no indication of interest or fit

conversationSummaries.notes: I spoke with a consultant from ZenC, who informed me that they are now a part of ZenSec after being acquired. They don’t handle CISO or VC roles and mentioned that my offering might not be relevant for their operations. I thanked them and wished them a good Friday.
